newsitem.title: USA: Reduced Eurodollar tick size draws mixed reactions.
newsitem.headline: Reduced Eurodollar tick size draws mixed reactions.

text.p: A halving in the minimum tick size for Eurodollar futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange drew mixed reactions as the market began quoting the first four quarterly months in the new size on Monday.
"It might take months in order to determine if it's effective in bringing in more volume," said a floor trader at a brokerage firm.
But he added that the first day of the initiative, aimed at increasing trades on slow days when bids and offers tend to get entrenched in a standoff, saw an above-average volume.

CME had been experimenting with a minimum price increment of half a basis point (0.005), worth $12.50, since the start of the year with the front month but decided last month to use it for the first four quarterly and two serial expirations from today.

"There was some good price movement during the course of the day, and the half-tick maybe at times accentuated people's willingness to trade and maybe scalp half a tick out," said John Nyhoff, vice president of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Futures Inc.
But Nyhoff and most other traders said the relatively good volume, estimated to be about 300,000 contracts, could well have been also a result of fairly wide trading range today.
The lead June contract closed 2.5 basis points lower at 94.185 after trading in a 94.195-94.160 range.

"It would be interesting in a couple of weeks on a Monday, when there's really no economic data coming out, to see whether there's more trading activity...or whether we simply have a tinier daily trading range," Nyhoff said.
Traders dealing with customers noted that they had to be more careful in working orders.

"It was certainly a disorienting experience," said a floor trader for an investment bank. He said he felt somewhat awkward when reading out quotes on the telephone. To flash a half-point tick between the pit and broker booths, a downward diagonal motion is used.
Some traders said the biggest concern was that it could make scalping, a big part of business for locals who make markets and provide liquidity in the pit, more difficult.
"The main fear in my mind is it could put undue pressure on locals and you end up trading paper to paper (customer orders) all the time," the investment bank trader said.
"From a liquidity standpoint it would be very negative if the locals got hurt by it, but hopefully they're making half a tick trading, as opposed to trading nothing," he added.
"I think it becomes more of an issue if they go quarter ticks," he went on. "I think the risk-reward on a $6.25-tick starts to become a substantially different proposition from a $25-tick value."

CME officials have said introduction of a quarter basis point tick was also being considered. Packages of different months, as well as spreads between a single month and a package, are already allowed to trade in quarter points.
